title: Telling your own story
goal: Bring everything in this course together into one complete story about yourself — your past, your present and your plans — in a single breath.
bekal: putting together a longer introduction: where you're from, where you live, work, experience, plans
the little flavor words that make your sentences sound Swedish
every verb form you've learned, in a single conversation

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Ett år senare
dialogs.intro: The following August. Dian stands at the front of a level-B Swedish class, introducing herself to a new group. Elin sits in the back row, listening in.

lines.speaker: Läraren:
lines.text: Berätta lite om dig själv, Dian.
lines.id: Tell us a bit about yourself, Dian.
lines.literal: tell little about you self, Dian.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag heter Dian och jag kommer från Indonesien, från en stad som heter Bandung.
lines.id: My name is Dian and I come from Indonesia, from a city called Bandung.
lines.literal: I am-called Dian and I come from Indonesia, from a city that is-called Bandung.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag har bott i Stockholm i ett år. Först bodde jag i Lappis, men nu delar jag lägenhet med en kompis.
lines.id: I've lived in Stockholm for a year. At first I lived in Lappis, but now I share an apartment with a friend.
lines.literal: I have lived in Stockholm in a year. first lived I in Lappis, but now share I apartment with a friend.

lines.speaker: Läraren:
lines.text: Vad gjorde du innan du kom hit?
lines.id: What did you do before you came here?
lines.literal: what did you before you came here?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag pluggade ekonomi i två år, och jag jobbade på ett café på helgerna.
lines.id: I studied economics for two years, and I worked in a café on weekends.
lines.literal: I studied economics in two years, and I worked at a café on weekends-the.

lines.speaker: Läraren:
lines.id: And why are you studying Swedish?

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Eftersom jag vill stanna. Jag tycker om Sverige, även om vintern är för lång.
lines.id: Because I want to stay. I like Sweden, even though the winter is too long.
lines.literal: because I want stay. I like about Sweden, even if winter-the is too long.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Mörkret i december. Och att folk inte pratar med främlingar på bussen.
lines.id: The darkness in December. And that people don't talk to strangers on the bus.
lines.literal: darkness-the in December. and that folk not talk with strangers on bus-the.

lines.speaker: Elin:
lines.text: Det gör vi aldrig. Det är inget personligt!
lines.id: We never do. It's nothing personal!
lines.literal: that do we never. it is nothing personal!

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Jag vet nu. Nästa år ska jag söka jobb här, och sedan får vi se.
lines.id: I know that now. Next year I'm going to apply for jobs here, and then we'll see.
lines.literal: I know now. next year shall I apply job here, and then get we see.

lines.speaker: Läraren:
lines.text: Det låter bra. Och du talar redan mycket bättre än för ett år sedan.
lines.id: That sounds good. And you already speak much better than a year ago.
lines.literal: that sounds good. and you speak already much better than for a year since.

lines.speaker: Dian:
lines.text: Tack! Det har tagit tid, men det har varit värt det.
lines.id: Thanks! It's taken time, but it's been worth it.
lines.literal: thanks! it has taken time, but it has been worth it.

notes: **Notice how many verb forms appear in this one short conversation**: present (*heter, kommer, delar*), past (*bodde, pluggade, jobbade, kom*), *har* + supine (*har bott, har varit, har tagit*), helper verbs (*vill, ska, får*), and a subordinate clause with BIFF (*att folk **inte** pratar*). You've learned all of them; this unit just puts them together.

**En stad som heter Bandung** — a very handy pattern for introducing something the other person doesn't know: *en stad som heter…* (a city called…), *en maträtt som heter…* (a dish called…), *ett ord som betyder…* (a word that means…).

**Även om** means "even though, even if" and introduces a subordinate clause, so BIFF applies: *även om jag **inte** förstår allt*. Its cousins *fast* and *trots att* mean the same; *fast* is the most casual, *trots att* the most formal.

**Det är inget personligt** explains something every newcomer needs to know: Swedes don't strike up conversations with strangers on public transport, in elevators or in lines. It isn't hostility — it's seen as **respecting other people's space**. Once you've been properly introduced, the warmth comes in full.
**Sedan får vi se** — "then we'll see". A fixed phrase for rounding off plans that aren't certain yet, and one of the most Swedish sentences there is: cautious, understated, promising nothing.
**Värt det** means "worth it" — the same words in the same order as English. *Det var värt det* is a good closing line for any story that was hard but turned out well.

grammars.title: A template for introducing yourself
body: These seven rows are a template you can use in class, at a job interview or around the dinner table. Fill in the right-hand column with your own life, learn it by heart, and you'll have a minute of Swedish ready to go at any time.

head: Content
Pattern
Example
rows: Jag kommer från… / Jag är från…
Jag har bott i Stockholm i ett år.
Innan jag kom hit pluggade jag i Bandung.
Nästa år ska jag söka jobb.

after: Notice that the third row uses *har bott* even though you still live there — the pattern from Unit 16, and exactly like English "I have lived here for a year". For how long you've lived somewhere, the standard pattern is *i* + a length of time: *i ett år*, *i sex månader*, *i tre veckor*.
The fifth row puts the subordinate clause first, so the main clause inverts: *Innan jag kom hit **pluggade** jag…* The verb-second rule from Unit 3 holds right up to the last page of this course.

grammars.title: Flavor words: what makes you sound Swedish

head: Word
Feel
Example
rows: after all, as we both know

after: None of the words in this table really translates, and none of them changes what the sentence means. What they change is the **tone** — and that is what separates someone who speaks Swedish correctly from someone who speaks it naturally. Think of what "actually", "like" and "I mean" do in English.
Start with **ju**, **nog** and **faktiskt**; they're the most common and the safest. Put them after the verb, in the same slot as *inte*: *Det är **ju** sant*, *Han kommer **nog** snart*.

sections.title: Thirty sentences that will take you anywhere

blocks.text: Only thirty — but between them they cover most of your everyday needs. Cover the left-hand column and test yourself.

head: Svenska
English
rows: I only speak a little Swedish.
What are you doing this weekend?

blocks.text: **Tyvärr** (unfortunately) deserves one last mention: it's a single word that softens any refusal, and Swedes use it constantly — at work, in shops, in text messages. *Jag kan tyvärr inte* is far gentler than *jag kan inte*, with no further explanation needed.

Twenty units are behind you. What you have now isn't just a list of words — you have correct sentence structure, four verb forms, two kinds of nouns, and an ear that is starting to tell *hw* from *sh*. That's a complete A1 foundation.

blocks.title: Three things to do this week
items: **Say one Swedish sentence to someone.** Just one. To a cashier, a neighbor, an online friend. A language that never leaves your mouth is never really learned.
**Lock the self-introduction template into your head.** The seven rows from the table a few pages back, filled in with your own life, memorized until they come out without thinking.

**Go back over Units 1, 4 and 15.** Between them they hold the three things that matter most: the one-form verb, the article on the end of the noun, and the past tense. Once those three are automatic, you're ready for A2.

blocks.text: Reread the *A1 grammar summary* and *The most common verbs* pages at the back of this course whenever you're unsure. Those two pages hold almost everything from the twenty units in a form you can take in at a glance.

And one last thing that isn't in any table: **Swedes will switch to English the moment they hear you hesitate** — and their English is excellent, which makes it all the more tempting to let them. It's kindness, not rejection — but it can stop you from ever making progress. There's only one rescue line, and you've known it since Unit 1: *Kan vi prata svenska? Jag övar.*

exercises.prompt: Full review. Fill in one suitable word.
items: Jag ____ Dian. (am called)
Jag kommer ____ Indonesien. (from)
Boken ligger ____ bordet. (on)
Han ringer ____ mamma. (his own)
Jag förstår ____. (not)
Göteborg är större ____ Malmö. (than)

exercises.prompt: Fill in the correct verb form of the word in brackets — present, past or supine.
items: Jag ____ i Stockholm i ett år. (har + bo)
Innan jag kom hit ____ jag ekonomi. (plugga, past)
Nästa år ____ jag söka jobb. (ska)
Jag ____ svenska varje dag. (öva, present)
Det ____ tid, men det var värt det. (ta, past)
Har du ____ surströmming? (prova, supine)

exercises.prompt: Join into one sentence using the linking word in brackets. Remember BIFF.
items: Jag läser svenska. Jag vill stanna här. (eftersom)
Jag tycker om Sverige. Vintern är för lång. (även om)
Jag ska söka jobb. Jag har klarat kursen. (när)
Jag vet det. Folk pratar inte på bussen. (att)
Ring mig. Du hinner inte. (om)
I've lived in Stockholm for a year.
Before I came here, I studied economics.
I'm studying Swedish because I want to stay.
Next year I'm going to apply for jobs here.
